title: Cycle of poverty

definition.text: A situation, also called a poverty trap, in which poverty seems to be passed down, so that later generations cannot escape it.

facts.text: Self-reinforcing mechanisms keep poverty going once it exists, unless someone from outside steps in.
Applied to developing countries, the same idea is called a development trap.
Lack of money, education and social connections all help keep poor families in the cycle.
Children are the most vulnerable, since they depend on guardians and are too young to work their own way out.
The cycle of poverty makes the harms of climate change worse.
People living in degraded ecosystems and a poverty trap may want sustainable options but cannot afford to let ecosystems and resources regenerate.
Conditional cash transfers aim to help poor families now and to break the cycle for the next generation by building their skills and health.

notes: Much of the page is about US social policy (minimum wage, schooling, incarceration); not used.

definition.text: The ways whole poor countries stay stuck in poverty, through causes such as lack of credit, environmental degradation, corruption, disease, war and poor infrastructure.

facts.text: Extreme environmental degradation is one cause, because it reduces how much farmland can produce.
Jeffrey Sachs argues the extreme poor lack six kinds of capital, including natural capital, and capital per person can fall each generation when population grows faster than savings.
Sachs argues that large, lasting foreign aid can raise the capital stock enough to lift households above subsistence.
He wants public money to go to health, education, infrastructure and natural capital such as conserving biodiversity and ecosystems, leaving business investment to private firms.

definition.text: An idea from development and environmental studies about how people, especially vulnerable groups, can support themselves in ways that last and can recover from shocks.

facts.text: It widens poverty studies beyond material want to include vulnerability and social exclusion.
The idea was introduced by the Brundtland Commission, and the 1992 UN Conference on Environment and Development made sustainable livelihoods a broad goal for ending poverty.
The approach seeks human-centered, participatory development that links concern for environmental and economic resources.
The UN Sustainable Development Goals, adopted in 2015 with 17 goals for 2030, are an example; the COVID-19 pandemic set back goals such as SDG 1, No Poverty.

title: Livelihood capitals framework

definition.text: The United Nations Development Programme's way of assessing livelihoods by the five kinds of capital people can draw on: human, social, natural, physical and financial.

facts.text: How much access people have to these assets shapes how the UNDP designs its development projects.
The approach also looks at how people use their assets to cope with shocks and stresses.
The UK's Department for International Development and CARE also use sustainable livelihood frameworks in place of sector-by-sector approaches.

notes: Requires 'Natural capital' from elsewhere in the course.

definition.text: A condition in which a person lacks the money and essentials needed for a basic standard of living.

facts.text: Absolute poverty compares income with what is needed for basic needs such as food, clothing and shelter; relative poverty compares living standards with others in the same time and place.
The 'dollar a day' poverty line, introduced in 1990, became US$1.90 a day in 2015, measured at purchasing power parity rather than exchange rates.
As of 2019, in PPP dollars, 85% of people lived on less than $30 a day, two-thirds on less than $10, and 10% on less than $1.90.
Poor people are more vulnerable to the environmental effects of industry, climate change, natural disasters and extreme weather.
Economic pressures on poor communities often play a part in deforestation and biodiversity loss.
Even when countries develop, the poorest citizens of middle-income countries often fail to gain enough of the new wealth to leave poverty.
Sustainable Development Goal 1, 'No Poverty', adopted by the United Nations in 2015, sums up the international framework for poverty alleviation.

title: Poverty and environmental degradation

definition.text: The two-way link between poverty and damage to nature: the poor suffer most from degradation, and some argue poverty itself drives it.

facts.text: The poor tend to suffer most from environmental degradation caused by exploiting natural resources.
About 92% of accumulated greenhouse gas emissions are attributed to Global North countries, yet developing countries suffer 99% of the casualties attributable to climate change.
This unfair split of environmental burdens and benefits gave rise to the global environmental justice and climate justice movements.

The Brundtland Report concluded that poverty causes environmental degradation, while the environmentalism-of-the-poor view holds that the global poor may be the most important force for sustainability.
A 2016 UN report claimed that by 2030 climate change could drive an additional 122 million people into extreme poverty.
Conservation can also burden the poor: fortress conservation has evicted indigenous people, and green colonialism grabs land in the name of environmentalism.

contested_note: The Brundtland Report says poverty causes environmental degradation, while the environmentalism-of-the-poor view sees the poor as a leading force for sustainability.

definition.text: The way degraded land and human deprivation reinforce each other, as falling land productivity cuts food, income and security.

facts.text: Land degradation brings lower crop yields, less food, more vulnerability to floods and droughts, people losing their homes, and economic problems.
It can reduce land's natural capacity to store and filter water, leading to water scarcity.

Southern Asia and sub-Saharan Africa are where degraded lands coincide with high poverty and childhood stunting; in 2025, 47 million stunted under-fives lived where stunting overlaps big degradation-driven yield losses.
Most of sub-Saharan Africa shows fairly low yield losses from degradation, not because soils are healthier but because poor access to inputs, machinery, credit and markets limits yields more.
Of the world's 570 million farms, 85% are under 2 hectares and work just 9% of farmland; farm size shapes farmers' ability to tackle degradation.
Soil degradation increases competition for farmland, and all but 3 conflicts inside African states since the 1990s are linked to such competition.
It can also drive environmental migration.

verification.title: Ensuring sustainable water security through sustainable land management: Research evidences for policy
verification.evidence: Land degradation is adversely affecting over 75% of the Earth's land surface and could exceed 90% by 2050.
verification.note: 75% of land surface affected; entry figures concern stunting and farms

definition.text: The link between lack of modern energy and lack of development, since businesses, public services and households all depend on energy.

facts.text: Poor energy access is associated with infant mortality, illiteracy and lower life expectancy, and can push people to move to cities.
Energy use and economic growth have historically risen together, though it is unclear which causes the other.
By the early 2000s rich countries were growing without a matching rise in energy use, but in developing countries the two stayed closely linked.
Energy-poor households often burn traditional biomass such as wood and dung, whose incomplete combustion releases black carbon, a health hazard.

definition.text: The pattern in which subsidies that make piped water cheap mostly help richer connected households, while many poor people go unserved.

facts.text: Water consumption subsidies go mostly to those connected to the supply grid, typically the richer, urban population outside informal housing.
With heavy subsidies, water prices in developing countries cover on average only 30% of supply costs.
Utilities then lack incentives to maintain or expand networks: leaks lose enough water for 200 million people a year, and many poor stay unconnected.
The poor instead buy from water vendors at about 5 to 16 times the metered price; subsidising new connections has shown more promise.
